title: Count ERROR lines per service in a log file
description: Read the application log and count how many ERROR-level lines each service produced. Return a dict with two keys: "error_counts", mapping each service name to its error count, and "total", the total number of error lines.
paraphrases: For each service in the application log, tally the ERROR-level entries, and also report the overall number of error lines. Return them under the keys "error_counts" and "total".

How many errors did every service log? Go through the app log, count the ERROR-level lines per service, and give the grand total as well. Put the per-service counts under "error_counts" and the total under "total".

title: Count HTTP 5xx responses per endpoint in an access log
description: Read the access log. Each line has five whitespace-separated fields: timestamp, HTTP method, endpoint path, status code, latency (e.g. "2026-03-02T09:14:06Z GET /api/orders 503 1200ms"). Count the responses whose status code is a server error (500-599 inclusive) per endpoint path. Return "errors_by_endpoint", a mapping of endpoint path to its 5xx count that includes only endpoints with at least one 5xx; "top_endpoint", the endpoint with the most 5xx responses, ties broken by the alphabetically smallest path; and "total_5xx", the total number of 5xx responses.
paraphrases: Go through the access log (fields: timestamp, method, path, status, latency) and count the 500-599 responses for each endpoint path. Return "errors_by_endpoint" (only paths with at least one 5xx), "top_endpoint" (most 5xx, ties to the alphabetically smallest path) and "total_5xx".

Which API endpoints are throwing server errors? From the access log, tally status codes 500 to 599 per path as "errors_by_endpoint" (leave out paths with none), name the worst one as "top_endpoint" (alphabetically first on a tie), and give the overall count as "total_5xx".

title: List the teams that own services with critical alerts
description: Query the monitoring alerts and the CMDB. Take every alert whose severity is exactly "critical", look its service up in the CMDB by name, and collect the owning team ("owner"). Services that are not in the CMDB are skipped. Return "affected_services", the distinct names of critical-alert services found in the CMDB, sorted alphabetically; "teams", the distinct owners of those services, sorted alphabetically; and "team_count", the number of distinct teams.
paraphrases: Join the critical alerts (severity exactly "critical") with the CMDB by service name and report which teams own the affected services. Skip services absent from the CMDB. Return sorted distinct "affected_services", sorted distinct "teams" (the CMDB owner) and "team_count".

Who needs to be paged? For each service with a critical alert that the CMDB knows about, find its owner. Give back the services as "affected_services" and the owners as "teams" (both de-duplicated and alphabetical), plus how many teams that is as "team_count"; ignore services the CMDB has no record of.

title: Find services that log errors but have no monitoring alert
description: Read the application log and query the monitoring alerts. A log line's level is its second whitespace-separated field and its service the third (e.g. "2026-03-03T08:00:05Z ERROR svc-mailer smtp handshake failed"); only lines whose level is exactly "ERROR" count, whatever the rest of the line says. A service is alerted if it has at least one alert of any severity. Return "error_services", the distinct services with ERROR lines, sorted alphabetically; "unalerted_services", those of them with no alert, sorted alphabetically; and "unalerted_count", the number of unalerted services.
paraphrases: Which services write ERROR-level log lines (level = second field, service = third) yet have no monitoring alert of any severity? Return sorted "error_services", sorted "unalerted_services" and "unalerted_count".

Look for monitoring blind spots: services that are logging errors but that nothing is alerting on. In each log line the second field is the level, which must be exactly ERROR, and the third is the service. Report every erroring service as "error_services", the ones without any alert as "unalerted_services" (both alphabetical), and how many blind spots there are as "unalerted_count".

title: First and last ERROR timestamp per service
description: Read the application log. Each line is "<timestamp> <LEVEL> <service> <message>", with timestamps in ISO 8601 UTC ("2026-03-04T11:02:10Z"). The log is not in chronological order. For every service with at least one line whose level is exactly "ERROR", find the earliest and the latest timestamp among its ERROR lines. Return "error_windows", a mapping of service to {"first": earliest, "last": latest}, with both timestamps copied exactly as written in the log; "services_with_errors", the number of such services; and "error_line_count", the total number of ERROR lines.
paraphrases: For each service that logged ERROR-level lines, give the earliest and latest timestamp of those lines as "error_windows" ({service: {"first": ..., "last": ...}}, timestamps verbatim from the log, which is unordered), plus "services_with_errors" (how many services) and "error_line_count" (how many ERROR lines).

When did each service start and stop failing? Using only lines whose level is ERROR, and remembering the log lines are shuffled, report per service the first and last error time under "error_windows" as {"first", "last"} (copy the timestamps exactly), how many services had errors as "services_with_errors", and how many ERROR lines there were as "error_line_count".

title: Deduplicate monitoring alerts and total their counts
description: Query the monitoring alerts. Alerts with the same service and the same severity are duplicates: merge each such group into one entry whose "count" is the sum of the group's counts. Return "alerts", a list of {"service", "severity", "count"} dicts with exactly those three keys, sorted by service then by severity (both alphabetically); "unique_alerts", the number of merged entries; and "total_count", the sum of all counts.
paraphrases: Merge duplicate monitoring alerts (same service and severity), summing their counts. Return "alerts" as [{"service", "severity", "count"}] sorted by service then severity, "unique_alerts" (number of merged entries) and "total_count" (sum of counts).

The alert feed is full of repeats. Collapse alerts that share both service and severity into a single entry carrying the combined count, list them under "alerts" (only the keys service, severity, count; ordered by service, then severity, alphabetically), and also report how many distinct entries remain as "unique_alerts" and the grand total of counts as "total_count".

title: Open one incident ticket for the most severe alert
description: Query the monitoring alerts and pick the single most severe one. Severity ranks critical > major > warning > info (this is a ranking, not alphabetical order); among alerts of the highest severity, take the one with the largest "count", and if counts tie, the alphabetically smallest service. Call create_incident_ticket exactly once for that alert, with a title naming its service. Return "ticket_id", the ticket id from the tool's response; "service", the chosen alert's service; and "severity", its severity.
paraphrases: Find the most severe monitoring alert (critical > major > warning > info; then highest count; then alphabetically smallest service), open exactly one incident ticket for it, and return "ticket_id" from the ticket tool, "service" and "severity".

Raise an incident for whatever is on fire worst right now. Rank alerts by severity (critical, then major, then warning, then info), break ties by the bigger count and after that by service name A-Z, file a single ticket for the winner, and report back its "ticket_id" (as returned by the ticketing tool), "service" and "severity".

title: Maximum and mean response latency per service
description: Read the application log. The service is the third whitespace-separated field of each line; some lines end with a field "latency_ms=<integer>" (e.g. "2026-03-05T14:00:01Z INFO svc-api GET /v1/items latency_ms=120"). Use only lines that carry a latency_ms field, whatever their level; ignore the rest. Return "latency", a mapping of service to {"max": the largest latency as an integer, "mean": the arithmetic mean rounded with round(x, 2)}; "slowest_service", the service with the largest max (ties broken by the alphabetically smallest name); and "samples", the number of latency values used.
paraphrases: From the log lines that carry "latency_ms=<n>", whatever their level, compute per service (the third field of the line) the max latency (int) and the mean rounded with round(x, 2), returned as "latency" {service: {"max", "mean"}}; also return "slowest_service" (largest max, alphabetical on ties) and "samples" (the number of latency values used).

How fast is each service responding? Only some log lines report a latency_ms value; using just those, give each service's worst and average latency under "latency" as {"max": int, "mean": two-decimal float}, name the service with the worst maximum as "slowest_service" (alphabetically first if tied), and say how many measurements you used, as a number, under "samples". The service is the third whitespace-separated field of each line.

title: Tier-1 services with a warning-or-worse alert
description: Query the CMDB and the monitoring alerts. Severities rank info < warning < major < critical (a ranking, not alphabetical order); an alert qualifies if its severity is warning, major or critical. Find the services whose CMDB "tier" is 1 and that have at least one qualifying alert; alerts for services not in the CMDB are ignored. Return "tier1_alerting_services", their names sorted alphabetically; "service_count", how many there are; and "alert_count", the sum of the "count" field over the qualifying alerts of those services (info alerts excluded).
paraphrases: List the CMDB tier-1 services that have at least one alert of severity warning, major or critical, sorted, as "tier1_alerting_services", with "service_count" and "alert_count" (sum of the counts of those qualifying alerts, info excluded). Ignore alerts for services missing from the CMDB.

Which of our most critical (tier 1) services are currently alerting at warning level or above? Check the CMDB tiers against the alerts, and return the matching service names alphabetically as "tier1_alerting_services", how many there are as "service_count", and the total of their warning/major/critical alert counts as "alert_count". Severity order is info, warning, major, critical.

title: Most frequent error message in a log
description: Read the application log. Each line is "<timestamp> <LEVEL> <service> <message...>"; the message is everything after the service field, with words joined by single spaces. Consider only lines whose level is exactly "ERROR", and count how often each message occurs regardless of which service logged it. Return "top_message", the most frequent message, ties broken by the alphabetically smallest message; "occurrences", how many times it occurs; and "distinct_messages", the number of different ERROR messages.
paraphrases: Among ERROR-level log lines, find the message text (everything after the service field) that occurs most often, across all services; break ties alphabetically. Return "top_message", "occurrences" and "distinct_messages".

What is the most common error in the log? Look only at lines logged at ERROR level, treat the text after the service name as the message no matter which service wrote it, and report the commonest one as "top_message" (alphabetically first if several tie), its count as "occurrences", and how many different error messages exist as "distinct_messages".

title: Normalise inconsistent date formats in a CSV
description: Read a CSV whose date column mixes ISO (YYYY-MM-DD) and European (DD/MM/YYYY) formats. Return a dict with two keys: "rows", every row with the date normalised to ISO, and "converted", the number of rows that needed conversion.
paraphrases: The date column of a CSV mixes YYYY-MM-DD and DD/MM/YYYY. Convert every date to ISO format, return all the rows, and say how many rows had to be converted. Use the keys "rows" and "converted".
Normalise the dates in a CSV file to ISO 8601 (some are written day/month/year), returning every row plus the number of rows you changed. Name them "rows" and "converted".

title: Sum transaction amounts per category from JSON records
description: Read the JSON dataset of transactions. Each record has an "id", a "category" (use it exactly as written) and an "amount" (a JSON number; negative amounts are refunds and must be included). Return "totals", a mapping of category to the sum of its amounts rounded with round(x, 2), and "grand_total", the sum of every amount in the dataset rounded with round(x, 2).
paraphrases: From the JSON transaction records, add up the amounts in each category (categories as written, refunds with negative amounts included) and also the grand total; return them as "totals" and "grand_total", each rounded with round(x, 2).

How much was spent per category? Go through the JSON dataset, total every category's amounts (negative refunds count too, category names verbatim) and give the overall sum as well, rounding everything to two decimals: keys "totals" and "grand_total".

title: Deduplicate CSV rows by id, keeping the latest
description: Read a CSV of account records with columns id, name, date and status (all values are strings; dates are ISO YYYY-MM-DD). Several ids appear more than once. For each id keep only the row with the latest date; if two rows for the same id share the latest date, keep the one that appears later in the file. Return "rows", the kept rows exactly as read (all four columns, string values), sorted by id compared as an integer in ascending order, and "removed", the number of rows dropped.
paraphrases: Remove duplicate ids from the CSV of account records (id, name, date, status; string values, ISO dates), keeping for each id the row with the latest date and, on equal dates, the later row in the file. Return the kept rows unchanged under "rows", ordered by id as an integer ascending, and how many rows were removed under "removed".

Some accounts appear several times in the CSV. Collapse them so each id has only its most recent record (by the ISO date; if dates tie, whichever comes later in the file wins), list the surviving rows as read in numeric id order as "rows", and report the number of discarded rows as "removed".

title: Quarterly totals from a spreadsheet, plus the best quarter
description: Read the sales spreadsheet. It has one sheet per quarter, named "Q1" to "Q4"; ignore any other sheet. Each quarter sheet's first row is the header ["region", "amount"] and every later row is [region, amount], where amount is a number or empty (null); skip rows whose amount is empty. Return "quarter_totals", a mapping of quarter sheet name to the sum of its amounts rounded with round(x, 2), and "best_quarter", the quarter with the highest total; if quarters tie, choose the earliest (Q1 before Q2, and so on).
paraphrases: The sales spreadsheet has a sheet per quarter (Q1 to Q4) plus possibly others to ignore; each quarter sheet starts with a ["region", "amount"] header and then [region, amount] rows, where an empty amount is skipped. Return each quarter's total under "quarter_totals" (round(x, 2)) and the quarter with the largest total under "best_quarter", earliest quarter winning a tie.

Which quarter sold the most? Add up the amounts on each of the Q1-Q4 sheets of the spreadsheet (skip the header row and any blank amounts, ignore sheets that are not quarters), give the per-quarter totals rounded to two places as "quarter_totals", and name the top quarter as "best_quarter", taking the earlier one if two are equal.

title: Normalise currency strings to USD amounts
description: Read a CSV with columns id and price (strings). Each price is either a symbol followed by a number ("$" = USD, "€" = EUR, "£" = GBP), or a number followed by a space and a currency code (USD, EUR or GBP). Numbers may use "," as a thousands separator. Convert every price to USD with these rates: 1 EUR = 1.10 USD, 1 GBP = 1.25 USD, 1 USD = 1 USD. Return "amounts", a mapping of id (the string from the CSV) to its USD amount rounded with round(x, 2); "total", the sum of those rounded amounts rounded with round(x, 2); and "converted", the number of rows whose original currency was not USD.
paraphrases: Convert the price strings in the CSV (id, price) to USD. Prices are written as a symbol and a number ($ USD, € EUR, £ GBP) or as a number, a space and a code (USD, EUR, GBP), possibly with "," thousands separators. Use 1 EUR = 1.10 USD and 1 GBP = 1.25 USD. Return "amounts" (id -> USD amount, round(x, 2)), "total" (round of the sum of the rounded amounts, 2 places) and "converted" (rows not originally in USD).

The price column mixes "$1,200.50"-style and "1200.5 USD"-style values in dollars, euros and pounds. Turn each into a US-dollar figure (EUR at 1.10, GBP at 1.25), keyed by the row's id string and rounded to cents, as "amounts"; add them up into "total" (rounded to cents); and say in "converted" how many rows were not already in dollars.

title: Validate email addresses in a CSV
description: Read a CSV of contacts with columns id, name and email (all strings). Check each email exactly as given, without trimming, against this rule: it is valid if and only if it contains no space characters, contains exactly one "@", the part before the "@" is non-empty, and the part after the "@" contains at least one "." and neither starts nor ends with ".". Return "invalid_ids", the ids (as strings) of rows with an invalid email, sorted by id compared as an integer ascending, and "valid_count", the number of rows with a valid email.
paraphrases: Validate the email column of the contacts CSV (id, name, email; strings) without trimming: an email is valid only if it has no spaces, exactly one "@", something before the "@", and after it a domain containing a "." that does not start or end with ".". Return "invalid_ids" (string ids, ordered by integer value) and "valid_count".

Which contacts have a bad email address? Using the CSV as-is (no whitespace stripping), call an email good when it has no spaces, a single @ with a non-empty name before it, and a domain after it that has a dot but doesn't begin or end with one. Give the ids of the bad ones, as the strings they are in the CSV, in numeric order as "invalid_ids" and how many are good as "valid_count".

title: Pivot CSV sales rows into region by month totals
description: Read a CSV of sales with columns region, month (YYYY-MM) and amount (a decimal string). Return "pivot", a nested mapping region -> month -> total amount for that region and month, rounded with round(x, 2), containing only the region/month pairs that occur in the data (no zero entries); and "regions_by_total", the list of regions ordered by their overall total (summed over all months) from highest to lowest, with ties broken alphabetically by region name.
paraphrases: Turn the sales CSV (region, month as YYYY-MM, amount as a decimal string) into a pivot keyed region -> month -> summed amount, rounded with round(x, 2), listing only pairs present in the data, under "pivot"; and under "regions_by_total" list the regions by their total across all months, largest first, alphabetical on ties.

Cross-tabulate the sales rows by region and month: for each region, the total sold in each month it appears in (rounded to cents, no empty months), returned as "pivot". Then rank the regions by overall sales, biggest first, resolving equal totals alphabetically, and return just their names, in that order, as the list "regions_by_total".

title: Join customers and orders sheets on customer_id
description: Read the spreadsheet. Sheet "customers" has the header ["customer_id", "name"] and sheet "orders" has the header ["order_id", "customer_id", "amount"]; every later row is data, ids are integers and amounts are numbers. Join orders to customers on customer_id. Return "summary", a list with one entry per customer (including customers with no orders), each {"name": <name>, "order_count": <int>, "spend": <sum of amounts rounded with round(x, 2), 0.0 if none>}, sorted by name ascending; and "unmatched_orders", the number of orders whose customer_id matches no customer.
paraphrases: Join the "orders" sheet (order_id, customer_id, amount) to the "customers" sheet (customer_id, name) of the spreadsheet on customer_id, skipping each sheet's header row. Under "summary" return one {"name", "order_count", "spend"} entry per customer, customers without orders included with 0 and 0.0, spend rounded with round(x, 2), sorted by name; under "unmatched_orders" give the number of orders with no matching customer.

For every customer in the spreadsheet, how many orders did they place and how much did they spend? Match the orders sheet to the customers sheet by customer id, list each customer by name in alphabetical order with "order_count" and "spend" (rounded to cents, zero for customers with nothing) as "summary", and count the orders that belong to no known customer as "unmatched_orders".

title: Monthly totals from CSV rows with mixed date formats
description: Read a CSV of payments with columns date and amount (strings). Dates come in exactly three formats: YYYY-MM-DD, DD/MM/YYYY (day first) and DD.MM.YYYY (day first). Amounts are decimal strings. Return "monthly_totals", a mapping of "YYYY-MM" to the sum of that month's amounts rounded with round(x, 2), containing only months that have at least one row, and "row_count", the total number of rows read.
paraphrases: Total the payments in the CSV (date, amount; strings) by month. Dates are YYYY-MM-DD, DD/MM/YYYY or DD.MM.YYYY, the last two day first. Return "monthly_totals" keyed "YYYY-MM" with round(x, 2) sums, only for months that occur, and "row_count", the number of rows.

How much was paid each month? The payment dates are a mix of ISO, day/month/year with slashes and day.month.year with dots; group the amounts by calendar month (key "YYYY-MM", rounded to cents, no empty months) as "monthly_totals" and say how many rows there were as "row_count".

title: Build a sales summary report and write it out
description: Read the JSON dataset of product sales; each record has "product" (string), "units" (int) and "unit_price" (number). Build a plain-text report whose lines are, in order: the line "Sales summary"; one line per product, sorted by product name ascending, of the form "<product>: <units> units, <revenue>", where revenue = units * unit_price formatted with two decimals (format "{:.2f}"), including products with zero units; and the line "Total: <sum of all revenues formatted with {:.2f}>". Join the lines with "\n" and no trailing newline. Write the report with write_report(path="sales_summary.txt", content=<report>). Return "line_count", the number of lines in the report, and "bytes_written", the "bytes" value the write_report tool returned.
paraphrases: From the JSON sales records (product, units, unit_price), build a text report: a first line "Sales summary", then "<product>: <units> units, <revenue>" for every product sorted by name (revenue = units * unit_price with "{:.2f}", zero-unit products kept), then "Total: <total with {:.2f}>", joined by "\n" without a trailing newline. Save it with write_report(path="sales_summary.txt", content=<report>) and return "line_count" (lines in the report) and "bytes_written" (the tool's "bytes").

Write up a short sales summary file: heading "Sales summary", one line per product in alphabetical order saying "<product>: <units> units, <revenue to 2 decimals>" (even when nothing sold), and a closing "Total: <grand revenue to 2 decimals>" line, newline-separated with none at the end. Hand it to write_report as content with path "sales_summary.txt", then report how many lines it has as "line_count" and how many bytes the tool said it wrote as "bytes_written".

title: Summarise which service owns which responsibility
description: Retrieve the available documentation chunks and produce a mapping from service name to the responsibility described for it, plus the number of services found, as a dict with two keys: "services" (the mapping) and "service_count". Each chunk reads "<service> handles <responsibility>."; key the mapping by <service> and map it to <responsibility>, both as written, without the final period.
paraphrases: Using the retrieved documentation chunks, map each service to the responsibility the documentation gives it, and count the services. Chunks read "<service> handles <responsibility>."; use <service> as the key and <responsibility> as the value, both as written, without the final period. Return the mapping under "services" and the count under "service_count".

From the documentation retrieval results, build a table of which service is responsible for what, plus how many services there are. Each chunk has the form "<service> handles <responsibility>."; key by <service>, map to <responsibility>, both verbatim, with the trailing period dropped. Keys: "services" for the table, "service_count" for the count.

title: List the documents that mention a keyword
description: Retrieve the documentation chunks and find every document that mentions the keyword "latency". A chunk mentions it when the text contains "latency" as a substring, compared case-insensitively ("Latency", "LATENCY" and "tail-latency" all count; "late" does not). Several chunks may share a doc_id. Return "doc_ids": the distinct doc_ids of the matching chunks, sorted in ascending string order, and "match_count": the number of distinct doc_ids in that list (not the number of matching chunks).
paraphrases: Retrieve the documentation chunks and identify each document mentioning "latency", matching the keyword as a case-insensitive substring. Return "doc_ids", the distinct doc_ids of matching chunks in ascending string order, and "match_count", the number of distinct doc_ids.

Which documents talk about latency? Search the retrieved chunks for "latency" in any letter case (also inside words like "tail-latency"), and give back the sorted, de-duplicated doc_ids as "doc_ids" together with how many documents that is as "match_count".

title: Build a glossary from definition chunks
description: Retrieve the documentation chunks and build a glossary. A chunk is a glossary entry when its text contains ": " (colon followed by a space); the term is the text before the first ": ", and the definition is the text after it, with surrounding whitespace removed and the single final period dropped (periods inside the definition stay). Chunks without ": " are ignored. If a term occurs more than once, keep the definition from the first chunk in retrieval order. Return "glossary", a mapping of term to definition (terms exactly as written), and "term_count", the number of distinct terms.
paraphrases: Retrieve the documentation chunks and compile a glossary from the ones of the form "<Term>: <definition>." — term before the first ": ", definition after it, trimmed, without the final period. Ignore chunks without ": ", keep the first definition when a term repeats, and return "glossary" (term to definition) and "term_count".

Turn the retrieved docs into a glossary. Some chunks define a term as "Term: definition."; split at the first ": ", keep the definition verbatim minus its trailing period, skip anything that isn't a definition, and if a term shows up twice the earlier one counts. Give back the term-to-definition map as "glossary" and the number of terms as "term_count".

title: Extract every ISO date from the documentation
description: Retrieve the documentation chunks and extract every date written as YYYY-MM-DD: four digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, two digits. A date that is the leading part of a timestamp such as 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z counts. Dates in any other format (for example 2024/01/20) and digit groups that do not have this exact shape (for example the ticket number INC-2024-0412) do not count. Return "dates", the distinct dates as strings sorted ascending, and "earliest", the earliest of them as a string.
paraphrases: Retrieve the documentation chunks and pull out every YYYY-MM-DD date, including the date part of timestamps but not dates in other formats or ticket numbers. Return "dates", the unique dates sorted ascending as strings, and "earliest", the first of them.

Go through the docs and collect all the ISO-style dates (four-digit year, two-digit month, two-digit day, hyphen-separated; a timestamp's date counts, slashed dates and ticket ids don't). Hand back the de-duplicated, ascending list as "dates" and the oldest one as "earliest".

title: Group extracted entities by type
description: Retrieve the shipment report chunks, run structured extraction over them, and group the extracted entities by their "type" field. Each value is stripped of surrounding whitespace and otherwise kept exactly as written (case-sensitive). Return "entities_by_type", a mapping from each type to the sorted (ascending string order) list of its distinct values, and "type_count", the number of distinct types.
paraphrases: Retrieve the shipment report chunks, extract structured entities from them, and group the entities by type. Strip whitespace around each value, de-duplicate, and sort each type's values ascending. Return "entities_by_type" (type to value list) and "type_count".

Pull the entities out of the shipment reports and bucket them by kind. Per type, list the distinct values (trimmed, case kept) in alphabetical order under "entities_by_type", and say how many kinds there are in "type_count".

title: Map each system to its owning team
description: Retrieve the ownership documentation chunks. A chunk may hold several sentences, separated by ". ". Only sentences of the exact form "<System> is owned by <Team>." assign ownership; other phrasings such as "maintained by" or "reviews" do not. Return "owners", a mapping from system to team, both exactly as written, and "top_team", the team that owns the most systems; if several teams tie, choose the one that comes first in ascending alphabetical order.
paraphrases: Retrieve the ownership documentation and map each system to its owning team, using only sentences of the form "<System> is owned by <Team>." (chunks may hold several sentences). Return "owners" (system to team, as written) and "top_team", the team owning the most systems, ties broken alphabetically.

Who owns what? Read the docs, and wherever a sentence says "X is owned by Y." record Y as X's owner; ignore "maintained by" and other wording. Give the system-to-team map as "owners", and name the team with the most systems as "top_team", picking the alphabetically first one on a tie.

title: Count policy rules by requirement level
description: Retrieve the security policy chunks. Each chunk's text consists of lines separated by a newline. A line is a rule when its first word (split on whitespace) is exactly "MUST", "SHOULD" or "MAY"; that word is the rule's level, so "MUST NOT ..." is a MUST rule. Level words elsewhere in a line, or in lower case, do not make a rule. Several chunks may share a doc_id. Return "rule_counts", a mapping with exactly the keys "MUST", "SHOULD" and "MAY" (zero if none) to the number of rules of that level across all chunks, and "most_must_doc", the doc_id with the most MUST rules summed over all its chunks; on a tie, the doc_id first in ascending string order.
paraphrases: Retrieve the security policy chunks and count the rule lines by level: a line whose first word is MUST, SHOULD or MAY (MUST NOT counts as MUST). Return "rule_counts" with keys MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and "most_must_doc", the doc_id with the most MUST rules over all its chunks, ties to the alphabetically first doc_id.

Tally the policy: every line that opens with MUST, SHOULD or MAY is a rule of that level (so MUST NOT is a MUST; a level word mid-sentence is not a rule). Report the per-level totals as "rule_counts" (all three keys), and which document carries the most MUST rules in total as "most_must_doc", alphabetical on a tie.

title: Map each claim to the documents that support it

title: Find the latest version of each product
description: Retrieve the release-note chunks. title: Extract an FAQ and write it as a report
